analysis.one_liner: Bars bankruptcy courts from erasing government lawsuits against corporate owners who never filed for bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill, written to stop wealthy owners from escaping lawsuits in a company's bankruptcy, never got a hearing or a vote and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company goes bankrupt, some courts currently let the company's owners, officers, or other people who never filed for bankruptcy walk away from lawsuits against them as part of the settlement plan. This bill would make that illegal when the lawsuits come from states, tribes, cities, or the federal government, allowing only a short 90-day pause. It was aimed at cases like the Sackler family's opioid settlement, where family members who didn't file for bankruptcy were released from liability. The bill was introduced in September 2023, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: States, tribes, cities, and the federal government would keep their right to sue wealthy owners and officers of bankrupt companies, and the victims those governments represent — such as people harmed by opioids — would keep a path to hold those individuals accountable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: States, tribes, cities, and crime/mass-tort victims

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends bankruptcy law so a court may not release or enjoin claims brought by a State, municipality, federally recognized Tribe, or the United States against a non-debtor, except through the existing asbestos-specific exception in section 524(g). [S3]
It allows only a temporary stay of up to 90 days on such government claims, so a bankruptcy case cannot be used to freeze accountability indefinitely. [S3]

The CRS summary explains the problem the bill targets: complex bankruptcies can release non-debtors like a company's officers and directors from liability, a practice that courts currently disagree about. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Owners, officers, and other insiders of bankrupt companies would lose their ability to get full protection from government lawsuits without paying for it; they would have to either settle those claims or remain exposed to them.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the current practice argue that third-party releases are often the price of getting wealthy insiders to contribute money to a bankruptcy estate; banning them could make some mass-injury settlements smaller or harder to reach, potentially delaying money to victims. The CRS summary notes the practice exists and that courts are split on it. [S2]
The bill is narrow: it protects only claims by governments, not lawsuits by private victims, so private plaintiffs could still be released from claims against non-debtors under current law. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it targets — government claims against non-debtors — the bill closes a genuine escape hatch, and the 90-day stay plus the asbestos exception show the drafters tried to limit disruption to legitimate bankruptcies. The strongest objection is real: taking third-party releases off the table can reduce the total settlement money on the table for victims. But the bill's protection is limited to government plaintiffs, so the problem it solves is only partly solved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal introduced the bill on September 18, 2023, joined by Sens. Warren and Welch. [S3]
That same day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary. [S5]
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 118th Congress. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy owners and officers of companies in bankruptcy are better off, because the current practice of releasing non-debtors from government lawsuits remains available in the courts that allow it — including in cases like the Sackler settlement the bill was named for.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners of bankrupt companies facing lawsuits

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SACKLER Act to bar non-consensual releases of government claims against non-debtors.

for.name: 2 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Sens. Warren and Welch), giving it its only Senate support.

against.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill received no further action after its referral.

against.name: The Sackler family and similar company owners
against.role: Beneficiaries of third-party releases in mass-tort bankruptcies
against.what_they_did: The bill was written to prohibit the kind of release the Sacklers received in the Purdue Pharma opioid bankruptcy; had it passed, family members would have remained exposed to state and federal lawsuits.

sides.party_line_note: All three Senate supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored or acted on the bill, but no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Owners and officers of companies facing mass-tort liability
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to exit government lawsuits through a company's bankruptcy without personally settling. Its namesake case is the Sackler family's opioid settlement. [S2][S3]

industries.industry: Corporations using bankruptcy to shed litigation (pharma, retail, and other large debtors)
industries.note: Companies could no longer offer owners and managers immunity from government claims as part of a reorganization plan, making such plans harder to sell and settle. [S2]
